Niacin, in its film-coated extended-release tablet form, is an antihyperlipidemic agent approved by the FDA for treating primary hyperlipidemia, mixed dyslipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and coronary arteriosclerosis. It is also used in combination with bile acid-binding resins for myocardial infarction prophylaxis. 2. Common adverse reactions to niacin include flushing, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, pruritus, and rash. 3. It is used to lower elevated total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), apolipoprotein B (Apo B), and triglycerides (TG), while increasing high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). 4. Niacin, in combination with simvastatin or lovastatin, is indicated for primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia when monotherapy with either agent is inadequate. 5. In patients with a history of myocardial infarction and hyperlipidemia, niacin is indicated to reduce the risk of recurrent nonfatal myocardial infarction. 6. In patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and hyperlipidemia, niacin combined with a bile acid-binding resin is indicated to slow the progression or promote regression of atherosclerotic disease. 7. Niacin is also indicated as adjunctive therapy for severe hypertriglyceridemia in adults at risk of pancreatitis who do not respond adequately to dietary efforts. 8. Niacin therapy should be initiated at 500 mg at bedtime to minimize the incidence and severity of side effects. The dose should be individualized based on patient response, with a recommended maintenance dose of 1,000 mg to 2,000 mg daily at bedtime. Doses exceeding 2,000 mg daily are not recommended. 9. Women may respond to lower doses of niacin compared to men. Single-dose bioavailability studies have shown that two 500 mg tablets are interchangeable with one 1,000 mg tablet, but other combinations of tablet strengths are not interchangeable. 10. Flushing of the skin can be reduced by pretreatment with aspirin (up to 325 mg taken 30 minutes before niacin) or by gradually increasing the niacin dose. Avoiding administration on an empty stomach and avoiding alcohol, hot drinks, or spicy foods around the time of ingestion can also help reduce flushing and pruritus. 11. Niacin should not be substituted for sustained-release or immediate-release niacin preparations at equivalent doses. Patients switching from other niacin products should follow the recommended titration schedule. 12. Niacin is contraindicated in patients with active liver disease, unexplained persistent elevations in hepatic transaminases, active peptic ulcer disease, arterial bleeding, or hypersensitivity to niacin or its components. 13. Niacin therapy should be used cautiously in patients with renal impairment, unstable angina, or during the acute phase of myocardial infarction, especially when combined with vasoactive drugs. 14. Niacin is rapidly metabolized by the liver and excreted through the kidneys. Liver function tests should be performed before treatment, every 6 to 12 weeks during the first year, and periodically thereafter. 15. Niacin therapy can increase fasting blood glucose levels, particularly in diabetic patients. Blood glucose should be monitored frequently, and adjustments to diet or hypoglycemic therapy may be necessary. 16. Niacin has been associated with small but statistically significant reductions in platelet count and increases in prothrombin time. Caution is advised when niacin is used concomitantly with anticoagulants. 17. Elevated uric acid levels have been reported with niacin therapy, so caution is advised in patients predisposed to gout. 18. Niacin has been associated with small, transient reductions in phosphorus levels. Periodic monitoring of phosphorus is recommended in patients at risk for hypophosphatemia. 19. Adverse reactions reported during clinical trials include flushing, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, increased cough, and pruritus. Flushing episodes were the most common treatment-emergent adverse reaction, reported by up to 88% of patients. 20. Niacin therapy has been associated with rare cases of rhabdomyolysis, particularly when combined with statins. Physicians should carefully weigh the benefits and risks of combination therapy and monitor for signs of muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness. 21. Severe hepatic toxicity, including fulminant hepatic necrosis, has occurred in patients substituting sustained-release niacin for immediate-release niacin at equivalent doses. Niacin should be used cautiously in patients with a history of liver disease or substantial alcohol consumption. 22. Niacin is classified as Pregnancy Category C. It is not known whether niacin can cause fetal harm when administered to pregnant women. If a woman becomes pregnant while on niacin therapy, the drug should be discontinued. 23. Niacin may interact with other drugs, including statins, bile acid sequestrants, aspirin, and antihypertensive agents. Caution is advised when niacin is used concomitantly with these medications. 24. Niacin may produce false elevations in some laboratory tests, such as plasma or urinary catecholamines and urine glucose tests.
